ECEA 5307 Linux Embedded System Topics and Projects

Instructor: Dan Walkes

Course Description

This course is used as the capstone in a three course sequence, including Linux System Programming and Introduction to Buildroot and Linux Kernel Programming and Introduction to Yocto Project. Both of these courses must be completed before starting this course.

This course builds on the content in the previous two prerequisite courses to develop a final project of your choosing targeting Linux device targeting hardware. The final project is delivered using concepts from Agile Scrum. Several pertinent, recent, and relevant Embedded System development related topics are covered as a part of the course curriculum, which you may optionally choose to incorporate into your final project.

Drops, Tuition Refunds, and Withdrawals

Because the MS-ECE has flexible course start dates, all drops, tuition refunds, withdrawals, and grades are handled at the individual course level. It is the student’s responsibility to monitor these deadlines. Coursera and CU Boulder are not responsible for notifying the students of these deadlines. You can drop or withdraw from a course via Your Programs & Enrollment Card via BuffPortal.

Drops and Refunds

Each student has 14 days from a class start date or their enrollment date (whichever is later) to drop for 100% tuition refund. Students are only eligible to drop a course if they have not accessed the restricted content (final exam or project). When a course is dropped under these conditions, it will not appear on the student’s record.

Students who access the final exam or project are assigned a grade and ineligible for a drop, withdrawal, or refund.

Withdrawal

Students may withdraw from a course after the 14-day period only if they have not accessed restricted content (final exam or project). In such cases, the course will not be eligible for a refund. When a student withdraws or does not complete the restricted content (final exam or project), a grade of "W" will be recorded on their academic transcript. This "W" grade does not impact the student's GPA or total earned credits.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance

Full AI Tool Usage: You may use AI tools in this course. Some assignments will require the use of such tools. However, keep in mind your own and others' privacy implications and security risks when using AI tools. If you use AI tools on assignments in CU Boulder courses hosted on Coursera, document your usage per the AI Usage Documentation Best Practices.

AI tools may not be used on the final exam.

AI Usage Documentation Best Practices

When using AI tools in your academic work, it is essential to accurately document how and why you used them. AI tools should be considered as aids rather than primary sources. Therefore, remember to:

  • Reference AI assistance. In your references or bibliography section, mention the AI tool used and the nature of its contribution. For example: "Assistance provided by [AI Tool Name] for generating initial content ideas, response to [prompt], [month, day, year]”.

  • Document your process. Save screenshots, dialog, prompt, queries or version history to document your process if you used AI. Include documentation in the submission if the assignment format allows. Otherwise, save it in your system in case you are asked by a program or university staff.

Suspected Violations of this Policy

If program staff suspects you may have used AI tools to complete assignments in ways not explicitly authorized or suspect other violations of the honor code, they will contact you via email. Be sure to respond promptly to any related communication so your perspective is included in the case review. Failure to respond timely will not prevent the completion of a case review.

Turnitin and similar AI detection tools may be used in these courses for initial detection of possible honor code violations. All suspected violations will be reviewed by a human. AI tools alone will not be used to determine if an assignment is plagiarized, and results from these tools will not be used alone as evidence to penalize students.

University Policies

Accommodation for Disabilities

If you qualify for accommodations because of a disability, please submit your accommodation letter to your program at msece-accomodations@colorado.edu in a timely manner so that your needs can be addressed. Disability Services determines accommodations based on documented disabilities in the academic environment. Information on requesting accommodations is located on the Disability Services website. Contact Disability Services at 303-492-8671 or dsinfo@colorado.edu for further assistance. If you have a temporary medical condition or injury, see Temporary Medical Conditions under the Students tab on the Disability Services website.

Classroom Behavior

Students and faculty each have responsibility for maintaining an appropriate learning environment. Those who fail to adhere to such behavioral standards may be subject to discipline. Professional courtesy and sensitivity are especially important with respect to individuals and topics dealing with race, color, national origin, sex, pregnancy, age, disability, creed, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, veteran status, political affiliation or political philosophy. Class rosters are provided to the instructor with the student's legal name. We will gladly honor your request to address you by an alternate name or gender pronoun. Please advise us of this preference early in the semester so that we may make appropriate changes to my records. For more information, see the Student Code of Conduct.

Honor Code

The University of Colorado Boulder takes issues of academic dishonesty extremely seriously. 

Students in all of CU Boulder’s courses, whether not-for-credit or for-credit, are expected to perform to the highest standards of academic honesty. 

Students enrolled in for-credit courses are members of the CU Boulder’s community and are subject to the Honor Code Office’s policies and procedures. Information on the Honor Code can be found at the Honor Code Office website.

Students who violate the Honor Code are subject to discipline. Violations of the policy may include: plagiarism, cheating, fabrication, lying, bribery, threats, unauthorized access to academic materials, submitting the same or similar work in more than one course without permission from all course instructors involved, and aiding academic dishonesty. Students are specifically expected to turn in original work and cite portions created by other authors. If a student has doubts regarding what collaboration is permissible in the course, the student should consult the discussion forums or the course facilitator directly.

Violations also include facilitating any act which may help a student to gain an unfair academic advantage including:

  1. Sharing course materials, including but not limited to personal notes, in an unauthorized online bank or forum, whether for profit or for free, is strongly discouraged and may result in a referral to the Honor Code. This includes sharing course materials on Slack.

  2. Sharing personal authentication credentials/login information to third party sites is strongly discouraged and may result in a referral to the Honor Code process

Sexual Misconduct, Discrimination, Harassment and/or Related Retaliation

The University of Colorado Boulder (CU Boulder) is committed to fostering a positive and welcoming learning, working, and living environment. CU Boulder will not tolerate acts of sexual misconduct, intimate partner abuse (including dating or domestic violence), stalking, or protected-class discrimination or harassment by members of our community. Individuals who believe they have been subject to misconduct or retaliatory actions for reporting a concern should contact the Office of Institutional Equity and Compliance (OIEC) at 303-492-2127 or cureport@colorado.edu. Information about the OIEC, university policies, anonymous reporting, and the campus resources can be found on the OIEC website. 

Please know that faculty and instructors have a responsibility to inform OIEC when made aware of incidents of sexual misconduct, discrimination, harassment and/or related retaliation, to ensure that individuals impacted receive information about options for reporting and support resources.

Religious Holidays

Campus policy regarding religious observances requires that faculty make every effort to deal reasonably and fairly with all students who, because of religious obligations, have conflicts with scheduled exams, assignments or required attendance. Since this is an online class, with no fixed weekly calendar schedule, we ask that you arrange your workload to accommodate your religious practice. See the campus policy regarding religious observances for full details.

AI Tool Guidance

Artificial intelligence tools—software that reproduces text, images, computer code, audio, video, and other content—have become widely available. Well-known examples include ChatGPT for text and DALL•E for images. This statement governs all such tools, including those released during your enrolled session. 

It is your responsibility—not the tool’s—to assure the quality, integrity, and accuracy of work you submit in all CU Boulder courses. Keep in mind that AI tools are designed to create content that seems to have been produced by a human, not to produce accurate or reliable content; therefore, relying on an AI tool may result in inaccurate content. Be wary of unintentional plagiarism or data fabrication. Act with integrity, for the sake of both your personal character and your academic record.

Consider the impact of using AI tools on your learning goals: in most cases, using an AI-generated answer without critical review and significant input from your end is contrary to the overall goal of personal learning and development in your chosen area.

Respect copyright and privacy. You may only enter your own data into AI tools. Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted data from others into AI tools without their consent. Avoid using AI for purposes that are private, sensitive, or high-risk.

Consider your environmental impact. Using AI models requires large amounts of electricity, water, and rare earth minerals. When using AI, keep in mind there are environmental concerns associated with its use.

You may use AI tools on assignments in this course as noted below.

Full AI Tool Usage

You may use AI tools in this course. Some assignments will require the use of such tools. However, keep in mind your own and others' privacy implications and security risks when using AI tools. If you use AI tools on assignments in CU Boulder courses hosted on Coursera, document your usage per the AI Usage Documentation Best Practices.

AI tools may not be used on the final exam.

AI Usage Documentation Best Practices

When using AI tools in your academic work, it is essential to accurately document how and why you used them. AI tools should be considered as aids rather than primary sources. Therefore, remember to:

  • Reference AI assistance. In your references or bibliography section, mention the AI tool used and the nature of its contribution. For example: "Assistance provided by [AI Tool Name] for generating initial content ideas, response to [prompt], [month, day, year]”.

  • Document your process. Save screenshots, dialog, prompt, queries or version history to document your process if you used AI. Include documentation in the submission if the assignment format allows. Otherwise, save it in your system in case you are asked by a program or university staff. 

Suspected Violations of this Policy

If program staff suspects you may have used AI tools to complete assignments in ways not explicitly authorized or suspect other violations of the honor code, they will contact you via email. Be sure to respond promptly to any related communication so your perspective is included in the case review. Failure to respond timely will not prevent the completion of a case review.

In suspected cases of unauthorized AI tool usage, the program may:

  • Request the documentation noted above (see AI Usage Documentation Best Practices) or other supplementary materials

  • Issue a warning

  • Assign a 0–50% grade for the question

  • Assign a 0–50% grade for the assignment

  • Assign an F grade for the course 

  • Reference prior violations

  • Remove access to the course, related materials, and tools

  • Contact the Office of Student Conduct & Conflict Resolution to report suspected Honor Code violations

Turnitin and similar AI detection tools may be used in these courses for initial detection of possible honor code violations. All suspected violations will be reviewed by a human. AI tools alone will not be used to determine if an assignment is plagiarized, and results from these tools will not be used alone as evidence to penalize students.

Non-credit learners are strongly encouraged to follow the guidelines above. If a non-credit learner upgrades to for-credit, they will be subjected to the above requirements.

System Requirements

You must have access to a computer configured with the following specifications to complete this specialization:

  • Operating System:

    • Ubuntu 22.04 (64-bit) is required.

    • Ubuntu 20.04 (64-bit) may also be used.

    • Other versions of Ubuntu, or other distributions, are not officially supported and may not work properly with assignment instructions.

    • The build system host must use an x86_64 (amd64) architecture. ARM-based systems are not supported.

    • Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) is not supported for ECEA 5306: Linux Kernel Programming and Introduction to Yocto Project, which includes Linux kernel development and Yocto projects. If you plan to continue to this course, please prepare a dedicated build host or virtual machine.

  • Memory (RAM):

    • At least 8 GB RAM is recommended.

    • You may be able to complete assignments with less, but 4 GB or less may cause build failures.

  • Disk Space:

    • At least 200 GB of free disk space is recommended.

Environment setup instructions are provided later in the course.

Hardware Requirements

Embedded hardware of a student’s choosing is required for the final project. 

  • Supported boards include:

    • Raspberry Pi (suitable for Buildroot & Yocto projects)

      • Raspberry Pi 4 Model B

        • SparkFun (Approx. $55)

      • Raspberry Pi 3 B+

        • SparkFun (Approx. $44)

      • Raspberry Pi ZeroW 

        • SparkFun (Approx. $17)

  • BeagleBone Black (suitable for Buildroot project)

    • BeagleBone Black Rev C

      • SparkFun (Approx. $70)

More information on final project hardware is provided in the Supported Hardware Platforms reading in the course wiki on GitHub.

Meet your course facilitators for Linux Embedded System Topics and Projects! They will be available to assist you during your learning experience by answering questions and offering weekly office hours over Zoom. Please click "Live Events" in the course menu on the left to participate in office hours.

To contact your course facilitator, email: msece-support@colorado.edu. Please include ECEA 5307 in the subject line!

GitHub Repository Links

Please find the link to create your repository for this assignment in the "GitHub Repo Creation Links" section under course resources. You may find course resources on the left side pane of your module view.

Implementation:

  1. You may implement the final project on your own, or organize in groups of up to 3 for this assignment.  All grading will be done individually based on your individual contribution to the project.  The total scope of the project should be the equivalent of at least 3 assignments (30-45 hours of implementation time per person) split as evenly between 3 sprints as possible.

  2. The link above will create an empty GitHub repository to store the individual portion of your assignment.

    1. For the Final Project Proposal submission you do not need to check any code into this repository.  However, you will add wiki pages and issues for each topic below.  

    2. Your final project repository will be publicly accessible (required for peer reviews).  

  3. The README.md in each student submission repository should link to a single “Project Overview” page in a single group member’s submission repository.  This is where the shared content related to the project will be created.

  4. The shared Project Overview wiki page should contain the following content, using this page (external link; opens in a new tab) as a template:

    1. An overview of the project goals and motivation.  Includes at least one diagram relevant to the overall project design which, at minimum, identifies the associated hardware.

    2. The target build system for the project, Buildroot or Yocto.

    3. The hardware platform selected.

      1. If using a hardware platform other than a platform listed as supported, links which detail how this platform can be supported by the build system of choice.

    4. Any open source projects (other than the current base platform Yocto/Buildroot packages used with assignments) intended to be used with the project.  If you intend to use no open source projects/packages please state this. Also add a link for each reference.

    5. Any previous assignment content intended to be used with the project.  If you do not intend to use previous assignment content, please state this.

    6. Previously discussed course content intended to be covered by the project implementation, and how this will be used in the project.  If you do not intend to use previous assignment content, please state this.

    7. Content not yet discussed or not covered in the course which is intended to be included in the project implementation and how this will be used in the project.

    8. If using the project with another course, the specific portions of the project which will be specific to this course (and implemented completely by you or your group).

    9. How you intend to organize the source code related to your project, especially for group projects:

      1. Which repository will hold the Buildroot or Yocto implementation (the suggestion is to use the project containing the Project Overview wiki page for this).

      2. Which repository/repositories will hold implementation scripts/source code for various project components

      3. Any additional repositories needed to store project content.

      4. Include the links to all repositories in your wiki with your submission.

    10. The team project members and the high level role of each project member in the overall project (group submissions only)

    11. A link to the shared schedule page (see detail below)

  5. A Schedule page linked from the Project Overview page and containing this content:

    1. Add your team members as collaborators to your final project GitHub repository created through the coursera instructions. Find instructions on GitHub (external link; opens in a new tab).

    2. One of the team members on your final project team should use the instructions in this Wiki page (external link; opens in a new tab) to create an Public empty repository in their personal GitHub account used to host a GitHub "Projects" page for your project. The Wiki page linked here should

      1. Please refer to this Reference Project (external link; opens in a new tab) for an example of the final layout of your Projects" page.

      2. All students in the team should be added to this repository as well to allow them to collaborate on the Projects page design. Find instructions for this step on GitHub (external link; opens in a new tab).

      3. Please link the Project created in this step to the Project Overview page for your final project

      4. Add links to issues in either the main project repository or individual student repositories tracking deliverables related to Sprint 1 items.

    3. At least one issue assigned to each student related to Sprint 1.

    4. All issues assigned include a complete Definition of Done (DoD), with sufficient detail to be understood by someone who is not a member of the project team.

    5. Any blockers between assigned issues are identified and linked.

    6. Tasks which have started include details about status.

    7. The top level schedule table is up to date with the content and status of individual issues.

Submission:

  1. Your submission in peer review must Include a Link to your (individual student) Final Project Repository which links to the overall project overview.

  2. Each student’s submission repository should contain a README.md pointing to the project overview page.

  3. The Project Overview page should contain all points referenced above (see the Assignment Peer Review rubric).

  4. Issues for at least Sprint 1 should be created as described in the schedule page, and include the content referenced above.

  5. The Schedule Page should be up to date and accurate.

Recent x86/x86_64 designs use bootloaders based on which architecture?

  • U-boot

  • UEFI

  • Redboot

  • BIOS

  • CFE

Which of the options below are possible reasons you may need a more complicated bootloader setup?

  • The system image may not fit in memory addressibly by inital boot code

  • Flash may require recovery, may not be linearly addressable

  • Hardware may require more complex setup

  • Software needs to run from RAM, which generally isn't possible with simple bootloaders

  • The reset vector boots to NOR flash, which is generally not accesible with simple bootloaders

The dtc utility is useful for

  • Applying device tree binary patches

  • Examining device trees

items.html:
Github Classroom Link (see final project proposal link)

Implementation:

1. Check in all code for the project to your project repositories.  Your code should build and run, and status of the build should match the status given in issues on your project repositories.

2. Update your Project Overview wiki page with any changes since the last sprint or since the original project proposal.   See Project Overview for the template (same one used for the project proposal assignment).  If/when editing, add an edit message describing the reason for the change.

3. Update your Schedule page (based on Project Template), linked from your Project Overview wiki page, to schedule issues for the next upcoming Sprint and close any issues completed in the previous sprint.  For multi-person groups, each group member is responsible for ensuring sprint issues are assigned to them and ensuring they’ve closed issues assigned to them resolved in the current sprint with appropriate detail included.  When necessary (if project overview sections have become out of date), students must update the project overview wiki page based on issues assigned to them.

  • Closed issues should be assigned to the group member who closed them, and updated by this group member.  At least one closed issue should be assigned to each member to track what they accomplished in the current sprint.

  • A comment in closed issues should mention that Definition of Done (DoD) is verified, with any relevant details including a general description or link to code changes made and description of testing which was performed.  The Definition of Done should be updated, if necessary, to match what was completed in the sprint.

  • If a sprint item is partially done, you should redefine the issue to include the portions already done, mark the item resolved in the sprint, move undone portions to a new item, and reference this item in the resolved issue as the follow-on task.

  • Issues should be assigned for each group member in the upcoming sprint with DoD defined.

  • Blockers should be identified and updated for closed and updated/new issues.

  • Use the “edit” option to edit the description and ensure it is up to date for each issue before closing.

Submission:

  1. Your Peer Review Submission Must Include a Link to your (individual student) Final Project Repository which links to the overall project overview. This is necessary for peer review assignment, also necessary so your reviewer can find your project.

  2. Code should be checked in corresponding to closed issues.

  3. At least one closed issue should be assigned (solely) to each project member.

  4. The Project Overview page should be updated as described above.

  5. Closed issues should include the detail mentioned above

  6. The Schedule Page should be up to date and accurate.

  7. For sprints 1 and 2: 

  • Issues for the next sprint should be created as described in the schedule page, and include the content referenced above.

  • Issues should be assigned to each group member for the upcoming sprint.

Given an asymmetric encryption step which requires a fixed input size, how can you sign a firmware image with different size?

  • Truncate your firmware image to match the required input size.

  • Use a hash function like SHA on the input firmware image to generate a fixed size output.

  • Only use the first or last bytes of the image as corresponding to the required input size.

Why is it important that a hash function used during a signature generation step produces different output with slight changes in input binary file?

  • It makes the public key more random

  • It ensures any small unauthorized changes in firmware payload result in a failure of signature validation steps.

What is one difference between a container and a virtual machine?

  • A virtulal machine does not have a dedicated root filesystem, shares the root filesystem with the host OS.

  • A container does not have a dedicated root filesystem, shares the root filesystem with the host OS.

  • A container does not have a dedicated kernel, shares the kernel with the host OS

  • A virtual machine does not have a dedicated kernel, shares the kernel with the host OS

How is the kernel namespace feature used to support application containers?

  • Enforce limits and constraints on process memory

  • Create a virtual isolated network instance used for the container

  • Combine multiple directories on the host into a single rootfs directory inside the container

How is the kernel control groups feature used to support application containers?

  • Create a virtual isolated list of process IDs used for the container

  • Enforce limits and constraints on process CPU

  • Combine multiple directories on the host into a single rootfs directory inside the container.

How is the kernel union mounts feature used to support application containers?

  • Enforce limits and constraints on process memory

  • Create virtual isolated ports used inside the container

  • Combine multiple directories on the host into a single rootfs directory inside the container.

The course final examination is similar in format to the homework quiz assignments, with the following important differences.

  • The exam is proctored. You will need to arrange a time to take the proctored exam. Please see the ProctorU Information reading for scheduling details.

  • The exam is 45 minutes long.

  • You are allowed 1 attempt.

    • An attempt is one complete try at the exam within the given time limit.

  • Each attempt allows 1 submission.

    • A submission occurs when you click “Submit” during an attempt. If multiple submissions are allowed, you may submit more than once within the time limit. Your last submission will determine your grade.

  • After the attempt window has ended, you will not be able to change or re-take the exam.

Permitted Exam Materials

You may use the following when taking the exam:

  • A notes sheet of paper, front and back, with 11pt or larger font if not hand-written. These notes must be your own and not copied from another student.

  • An electronic copy of your notes sheet, if you prefer this to a physical paper.

  • One URL containing your notes (for example, a Google Drive link or similar online editor).

  • Pens, pencils, blank paper as desired.

Prohibited Exam Materials

You may not use the following when taking the exam:

  • Course textbooks.

  • Lecture slides and lecture content.

  • AI Tools.

You may drop or withdraw from this course at any time before accessing the final exam. Once you begin the exam, you will be assigned a course grade based on the announced grading formula, and this grade will appear on your university transcript after the eight-week session concludes. After the final exam has ended, you may continue submitting homework assignments until the conclusion of the eight-week session.

How ME-ECE Uses Virtual/Remote Proctoring

Most for-credit MS-ECE courses feature a proctored experience at the end of the course. This is generally an exam, but may also be a project-based experience. The University of Colorado Boulder takes academic integrity seriously, and is committed to ensuring that your MS-ECE degree accurately represents your competency and retains its value in the marketplace. Protecting the integrity of the course exams is part of this process.

The stakes of the proctored experiences in MS-ECE courses are high. When you gain access to these protected items on the Coursera platform, you are no longer eligible for a tuition refund if you decide to drop the course, and you are no longer eligible for a course withdrawal. Accessing the protected examination means that you will only be eligible for an earned grade based on performance.

What is ProctorU?

ProctorU is a platform that is partnered with your institution to help you take an exam online while ensuring academic integrity is upheld. Using this platform allows you the convenience of testing from home 24/7, 365 days a year. 

How it Works

  1. Create a ProctorU account.

    1. Click here to get started.

  2. Download the Guardian Secure Browser.

  3. Schedule at least 72 hours in advance of the date/time you want to take your exam.

    1. Login and click the “Schedule New Session” button.

    2. Confirm your institution, term, and exam name, then click “Search Sessions.”

    3. Use the calendar and clock features on the left to select your desired testing date and time.

    4. Click here to log in to your ProctorU account and test your equipment.

  4. Click here to log in to your ProctorU account and test your equipment.

  5.  Know What to Expect. See below for more information:

    1. 5 Steps for Student Guide

    2. Video: Student Experience for Colleges and Universities – explains what you will need and what’s expected before and during your exam

Important Reminders

Note: Last Day and Time to Schedule ProctorU Exam will always be 3 days prior to the end of the session. It will always fall on a Tuesday, 4:50pm MT.

We strongly recommend that you do not start the proctored exam process until you are ready to take the exam and complete the course. Find more details about the relationship between proctored experiences and course drops/refunds in the MS-ECE on Coursera Student Handbook.

  • You will be able to take final exams for MS-ECE courses using the ProctorU remote proctoring service between 9:00 am Mountain Time on the day session starts until 4:50 pm Mountain Time on the day your class session ends.

  • You must schedule your exam at least 72 hours in advance of your desired day and time. For example, if the exam availability window closes at 4:50 pm on a Friday, the last time you could schedule an exam would be that Tuesday at 4:50 pm.

  • To secure your desired exam session time, log into ProctorU and schedule your session as soon as you know your desired exams session date and time.

  • View the Academic Calendar for your session to see final exam availability. Test Your Equipment before exam day in an environment that is identical to where you are planning to take your exam.

Equipment Requirements

  • A computer

  • A reliable internet connection – if connectivity is lost during an exam, you may not be able to regain access

  • A webcam

  • A microphone

  • Two forms of photo ID – one form should be a government-issued photo ID; the second form of ID is recommended though not required

  • A reflective surface handy

Here are some important caveats and limitations to keep in mind when testing:

  • You will not be permitted to test with remote control software running on your computer. Applications like TeamViewer, GoToMyPC, AnyDesk, etc.

  • You will only be permitted the use of a single monitor when testing, all others must be disconnected.
